name: Grebo
confidence_why: Innes (1966), following Berry and Innes (1957), describes two degrees of stress in Grebo with word pairs distinguished by stress placement alone (sono 'sting' vs so'no 'smell'), but Newman (1986), working with a single Cape Palmas speaker, could not verify the stress phenomena Innes describes and left open whether the discrepancy was his speaker's idiosyncrasy, so the lexical-stress reading rests on Innes's fuller in-field description against one hedged challenge.
catalog_citation: Innes, Gordon (1966). An Introduction to Grebo. London: School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London (printed by Mouton, The Hague). Carried via the StressTyp2 entry(source 684); corroborating snippets from Google Books volume T-AtAAAAMAAJ…
catalog_quote: [StressTyp2 passage 1013, citing Innes (1966:19)] Stress in Grebo is a complex of phonetic features, some of which are very difficult to describe precisely, but others, such as lengthening of consonants, are more readily described. Two degrees of stress are rcognised, 'strong' (maximal) stress, and 'zero' stress. Words can be differentiated only by the place of the stress. There are three styles of pronunciation: Unemphatic and Emphatic 1 and 2. ... [Google Books snippets, Innes 1966 pp.18-19] There is an important characteristic of Grebo speech which can conveniently be called stress. ... Unemphatic Pronunciation (UP), Emphatic Pronunciation 1 (EP1), and ... stressed also in EP1, but is front-stressed in EP2. All disyllabic nouns and verbs bear one strong stress, and most of the former occur with all three styles of pronunciation ... [Google Books snippet, van der Hulst et al. 2010 Survey, Gr…

Umiker-Sebeok (eds.) 1976, Speech Surrogates: Drum and Whistle Systems, Part 1, 553-573, The Hague: Mouton, DOI 10.1515/9783110804416.553.]
tone_statements.quote: It is a tone-language ... Besides the four basic tones, which are independent phonemes, there are a number of quick glides, falling or rising between various of the four tones. Some of these are phonemic, some morphophonemic, some positional variants of the four tones; their time-value is equal to that of a single mora, and syllables which carry them count as single morae. ... In the present study, the four registers are represented by the numbers 1 to 4, descending from the highest to the lowest.
tone_statements.locator: p. 223 ('It is a tone-language'), p. 224 (cursory sketch of Jabo phonetics) and p. 225 fn. 12 (register numbering), section 'The technique of Jabo drum-signaling'
tone_statements.summary: Jabo is a tone language: four register tonemes (1 highest to 4 lowest) inherent in every syllable/mora, plus quick glides, some phonemic; much grammatical tone; neighbouring Grebo said to have three.

tone_statements.citation: Herzog, George. 1934. Speech-melody and primitive music. The Musical Quarterly XX(4): 452-466. DOI 10.1093/mq/XX.4.452. (Oxford Academic landing: academic.oup.com/mq/article/XX/4/452/1201932.)
tone_statements.quote: [p. 453] that of the Jabo in Eastern Liberia assigns to the syllable ba four totally unrelated meanings, depending on its pitch. Spoken on high pitch, ba means "namesake"; on a somewhat lower pitch, it means "to be broad"; in the middle register, it means "tail"; and spoken quite low, it is a particle expressing command. ... [p. 453] with inflection falling from high to middle, it means "it is a namesake". ... [p. 454] The Jabo language of Western Liberia, as we have seen, employs four "tones" or registers. ... [p. 455 register key:] ( ´ for "high tone"; ¯ for "normal", the register next below; ' for "middle tone"; ` for "low tone".)
tone_statements.locator: pp. 453-454, opening of the Jabo discussion; register labels p. 455
tone_statements.summary: Four tone registers (high, 'normal', middle, low) distinguish words, shown on the syllable ba; also a long high and a high-to-mid falling inflection; pitch shifts regularly with adjacent syllables.

audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: the the StressTyp2 entrytext and its source row 684 (= Innes 1966) are verbatim in the held SQL dump, and every Innes 1966 / Survey 2010 snippet fragment in the record is verbatim in the copies we hold; but Innes 1966 pp.18-19 themselves are not yet obtained (Rosetta excerpts stop at p.15), so the check is against the carrier, hence quotation partly verified. (2) Deciding source: effectively StressTyp2 quoting Innes 1966, a SOAS descriptive grammar that is the fullest description of the language and the only Glottolog 'grammar'; Berry & Innes 1957 (snippet downloaded now) gives the same two-degree, three-style stress analysis, and a 1975 MSU working paper reuses it as a 'stress reversing rule'. Languoid identity checks out (Berry & Innes place their Grebo on the Fishtown-Cavalla coast = Glebo, Southern Grebo), even though StressTyp2 filed the lect under grv. (3) New finding: Newman 1986, the onl
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again.— I re-opened every held piece and the compilers finding stands. (1) StressTyp2 dump line 28753: row (1013, 684, NULL, 'Stress in Grebo is a complex of phonetic features.. Two degrees of stress are rcognised, strong (maximal) stress, and zero stress. Words can be differentiated only by the place of the stress. There are three styles of pronunciation: Unemphatic and Emphatic 1 and 2 (see remarks). Innes (1966:19).'; line 50489: source 684 = 'Innes, Gordon (1966). An introduction to Grebo. London: SOAS'. Verbatim match to the record's quote (typo 'rcognised' is StressTyp2's).
